content: Nebulised surfactant has the potential to deliver surfactant directly to the lungs of preterm infants. This approach aims to avoid the need for endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation, which are associated with ventilator-induced lung injury and bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD). The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of nebulised surfactant, either as a preventive measure or as a treatment, compared to placebo, no treatment, or intratracheal surfactant administration, on morbidity and mortality in preterm infants with or at risk of respiratory distress syndrome (RDS). A comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL, covering studies up to January 2012. Additional sources such as conference proceedings, clinical trial registries, Google Scholar, and reference lists of identified studies were also reviewed. Experts and surfactant manufacturers were contacted to ensure thorough coverage. The inclusion criteria focused on randomised, cluster-randomised, or quasi-randomised controlled trials comparing nebulised surfactant administration to other interventions in preterm infants at risk of RDS. Both published and unpublished studies, as well as ongoing trials, were considered. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility and quality of the studies and extracted relevant data. However, no studies were identified that investigated the prophylactic or early use of nebulised surfactant. Only one small study, which examined late rescue nebulised surfactant, met the inclusion criteria. This study involved 32 preterm infants born before 36 weeks of gestation who were diagnosed with RDS and were receiving nasal continuous positive airway pressure (nCPAP). The study was determined to have a moderate risk of bias. The results of this single study showed no significant differences between the group receiving nebulised surfactant and the no-treatment group in terms of chronic lung disease (risk ratio [RR] 5.00; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.26 to 96.59) or other outcomes, such as oxygenation within 1 to 12 hours after randomisation, the need for mechanical ventilation, the duration of mechanical ventilation or CPAP, or the number of days requiring supplemental oxygen. Importantly, no adverse effects related to nebulised surfactant therapy or aerosol inhalation were reported. The authors concluded that there is currently insufficient evidence to support or refute the use of nebulised surfactant in clinical practice. Larger, well-designed trials are necessary to determine the efficacy of nebulised surfactant for the prevention or early treatment of RDS in preterm infants. Until such evidence is available, the use of nebulised surfactant should be restricted to clinical trials.
